title: Quality of Information in YouTube Videos on Erectile Dysfunction
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the first 100 English YouTube videos returned for 'erectile dysfunction'. Besides DISCERN/PEMAT quality scores, the authors explicitly rated misinformation (defined as contradictions of established literature and/or guidelines) and report the share of videos containing it: 26/92 (28%). That is a CONTENT prevalence estimate with an external ground truth (literature/guidelines) and a stated denominator.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language YouTube search, not logged in; authors based in Denmark/Italy/Belgium)
estimates.date: Search performed October 2019; videos posted 13 May 2008 - 6 August 2019
estimates.measure_type: % of YouTube videos with medical information on erectile dysfunction judged to contain direct misinformation
estimates.denominator: 92 of the first 100 English-language YouTube videos returned for 'erectile dysfunction' (relevance-sorted) that contained medical information
estimates.definition: Video rated as containing 'direct misinformation', i.e. content contradicting established literature and/or guidelines, at any level above 'none' on a 1-5 Likert scale (none/low/moderate/high/extreme)
estimates.misinfo_def: 'we rated the extent of misinformation (defined as contradictions of established literature and/or guidelines) of the videos on a Likert score of 1-5 with the numbers corresponding to "none," "low," "moderate," "high," or "extreme."'
estimates.source_quote: Overall, 28% of the videos contained direct misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 410 (also Abstract: 'Overall, 28% of the videos contained direct misinformation')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Videos evaluated by 3 of the authors - 2 medical doctors with a special interest in ED/andrology and 1 research fellow without specialised knowledge; assessors familiarised themselves with the PEMAT user's guide and DISCERN handbooks; disagreements settled by discussion and consensus. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported. Misinformation was judged against established literature and clinical guidelines.
estimates.moderator_quote: We searched the term "erectile dysfunction" on YouTube in October 2019 (not logged into any personal account) without filters and sorted by relevance in the search function. We evaluated the first 100 videos in English and noted if they contained medical information, defined as material about biological mechanisms
estimates.notes: The Results sentence carrying the counts reads 'Overall, 26/92 (28%) videos with medical information were deemed to contain direct misinformation. In 8 cases, the level of misinformation was low; in 11 cases, it was moderate; in 3 cases, it was high; and in 3 cases, it was deemed extreme.' - it is split across interleaved PDF columns in the text rendering, so the contiguous verbatim span quoted in source_quote is the Abstract's version of the same finding. Rank-truncated set (first 100 relevance-sorted results) hence denom_selection=curated. Denominator is the 92 videos containing medical information, not all 100 retrieved (28% of all 100 would also be 28% only by coincidence of rounding; the paper's abstract loosely says '28% of the videos'). Internal inconsistency worth flagging: the level breakdown sums to 25 (8 low + 11 moderate + 3 high + 3 extreme), one short of the stated 26; the headline 26/92 (28%) is the verbatim value kept here.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same three assessors (2 MDs specialised in ED/andrology, 1 non-specialist research fellow) applied the validated DISCERN instrument and PEMAT for audiovisual materials; disagreements settled by discussion and consensus; no reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: All videos containing medical information underwent a systematic evaluation using the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Audiovisual Materials (PEMAT) and the validated DISCERN quality criteria for consumer health information.
estimates.notes: source_quote stops at the line break because a control character sits between 'receiving a' and 'score of 3.' in the text rendering; the full Abstract sentence is 'The median DISCERN score was 2 (range 1-5) with 80.4% receiving a score of 3.' and the Discussion states 'the information may be of varying value as illustrated in our study by more than 80% receiving a DISCERN score of 3 or less signifying low to moderate overall quality.' QUALITY row per the codebook (DISCERN score, not a falsity judgement) - kept for the appendix, excluded from prevalence. A wholly accurate video can score low on DISCERN (e.g. for not citing sources or omitting alternatives), so this is not a misinformation share. The abstract's wording '80.4% receiving a score of 3' appears to be a typo for 'a score of 3 or less': the Discussion says 'more than 80% receiving a DISCERN score of 3 or less' and Table 3's cumulative 19.6 + 38 + 22.8 = 80.4.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted (not truth/falsity measures, and not misinformation shares): 22% of videos attempted to sell specific products; commercial bias 23/92 (25%); complementary/alternative medicine 20/92 (21.7%); new technology 13/92 (14.1%); producer mix (42% professional medical institutions, 21% individual medical professionals, 37% non-medical YouTubers); audience mix (53% general public, 40% ED patients, 7% health-care professionals); 92% of the 100 videos contained medical information and 67% contained treatment information; 25 of 97 comment sections contained advertising. The PEMAT understandability/actionability medians are scale medians, not shares, so no row. The severity split within the misinformation-positive videos (low/moderate/high/extreme) was not split into rows: those are within-misinformation composition and they sum to 25 rather than the stated 26.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Sampling frame: the first 100 English-language YouTube videos returned for the query 'erectile dysfunction' in October 2019, not logged in, no filters, sorted by relevance - a rank-truncated convenience frame with no random sampling and no time-stability check. 92 videos containing medical information were assessed with PEMAT (audiovisual), DISCERN and an author-devised 1-5 misinformation Likert. Three assessors (2 ED/andrology MDs, 1 non-specialist research fellow); disagreements resolved by discussion and consensus; NO inter-rater reliability statistic is reported and the authors name subjective evaluation and observer bias as the main limitation. Denominator for the misinformation share is clearly stated (92 videos with medical information).
